RECREATION CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES

Outdoor recreation is an important sector in Arkansas that touches many other business sectors. It is very much a
part of the state's identity and culture. Given how vital outdoor recreation is to the state's identity and continued
economic prosperity, SCORP identifies the state's top four priorities for outdoor recreation to ensure that it
continues to grow successfully. Those priorities are connectivity, community, innovation, accommodation, and
stewardship. SCORP also details the top five barriers that are negatively impacting parks and open spaces across the
state, hindering participation in outdoor recreation. These are: Income Inequality, Physical Impairment, Lack of Free
Time, Nobody to Go With, and Feeling Unsafe. SCORP suggests addressing these hindrances through four points:

     · Understanding how different barriers can impact outdoor recreation.
     · Reviewing which barriers have been identified in the SCORP.
     · Investigating your community to identify existing barriers.
     · Engaging your community to create an action plan for removing these barriers and preventing future

          barriers from occurring.

Demographic Opportunities
While there are challenges for outdoor recreation, there are also trends that point to opportunities. In the last few
years, there has been a recognizable increase in the 65 years and older population in Arkansas and throughout the

                                                                                                                                          16
Recreational Trends Research (Task 1.4) Draft
United States. Even in Fayetteville, the 65+ age group accounts for 10.1% and is expected to grow the fastest of any
age segment, accounting for 11.2% of the population by 2025. This increase will impact how parks and recreation
facilities are programmed in the future. People over the age of 65 tend to gravitate toward opportunities for
socialization and serving their larger communities. Focusing on providing recreational and outdoor opportunities for
these residents, especially to help them stay healthy and active, has the potential to infuse parks and open spaces
with dedicated participants who can help teach the next generations how to be good stewards of our public spaces.

The fact that in 2019, more than 16,000 adults in Fayetteville were expected to spend more than the national
average on sports and recreation equipment provides an opportunity to continue to educate residents and visitors
on the importance of these spaces, encouraging volunteer and conservation efforts, and providing opportunities for
people to spend even more time outdoors. Utilizing public/private partnerships to support and enhance outdoor
recreation is another opportunity to provide a safety net when and if one type of funding for parks and open spaces
might not be available.

The economic findings of spending in the future 2024-2028 SCORP may show a dramatically different reality and
projection of spending based on the unanticipated outcomes of COVID-19, with more people spending time
recreating close to home, but also taking up new recreational pursuits or upgrading existing ones. For example,
bicycle sales and repairs to older bicycles soared in 2020, which is not represented in the data reported.

Minority Groups Challenges and Opportunities
Following up on some data from the state's SCORP report, there seems to be some opportunities to better engage
minority groups and promote recreational offerings in a more equitable and just way. From a racial/ethnic
standpoint, the report highlights how certain activities have noticeably different participation rates between Whites
and African Americans. The difference between participation rates between Blacks and Whites can be more than
40% in activities like visiting lakes and swimming. As barriers for recreation, significantly more African Americans
than Whites expressed concerns regarding not knowing where to go, a lack of gears or equipment, safety concerns,
and needing to learn more or develop skills to do a certain activity. The report also highlights the concerns of
individuals with impairment citing that 27% of their respondents reported some sort of impairment. The report
states that among these respondents, participation levels were lower across all types of outdoor recreation
activities. Lastly, there's also a section that deals with the gender gap when it comes to certain recreation activities.
The City of Fayetteville could make use of all this information to make better decisions on how to develop their
parks and open space to better serve different populations.

The Impact of Covid-19
The coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic will have a lasting impact on people and how they have come to rely heavily
on close-to-home access to nature and outdoor recreation, and there will be an on-going evolution of
understanding the impact and impression of the virus on the public as it relates to public spaces. Parks and trails act
as critical infrastructure to the public, serving physical, mental, and emotional needs, and as such, opportunities for
the City exist for public services. Opportunities to respond to the lingering affects of the pandemic include:

      · flexible, adaptive and expansive outdoor spaces for classes and programming that cannot safely be
           provided indoors;

      · trails to fill gaps in public transportation;
      · addressing overcrowding by expanding resources in high demand areas and raising awareness of and

           spreading the love to less popular locations;
      · distanced activities and addressing social isolation for vulnerable populations; and
      · youth being disconnected from sports and athletics, fear in managing physical interactions in youth sports,

           and underserved populations facing the inability to `pay-to-play'.

The Sports and Fitness Industry Association (SFIA) survey of membership in June of 2020 showed that 72% of
respondents expect individual sports and 66% anticipate outdoor sports to be the two top product categories to
return to health post-COVID-19. Only 37% of respondents anticipate that the return of youth sports will return in
2021 or later.29 The NRPA Youth Sports at Park and Recreation Agencies report also stated that 90% of park and

                                                                                                                                          17
Recreational Trends Research (Task 1.4) Draft
recreation professionals report that the pandemic had a significant detrimental impact on their agencies' youth
sports programming during the summer and fall of 2020.30

Trends in Priorities
Fayetteville will also be taking cues from SCORP and identify its own priorities for outdoor recreation, potentially
aligning with the state's goals. A SCORP survey requested outdoor recreation agencies/organizations to do a park
assessment and take a survey on park priorities and performances for the future. The items that were voted as top
need or priority were: new facility development (13.5%), adequate staffing (10.3%), updating/renovating facilities
(8.3%), maintenance (buildings, roads, infrastructure) (3.8%), accessibility improvements (5.8%).

MEMORANDUM PURPOSE

This interim internal report is intended to capture all currently available data on the City of Fayetteville's Community
Profile that is relevant to outdoor recreation and analysis of what this means for recreation planning. Tasks also in
progress or completed include review of existing documents memo (complete), recreation trends memo (in
progress) and the parks classification and level of service (in progress). The compilation of these four memos will
represent an understanding of the Existing Conditions and Opportunities in Phase 1 of work. Key information from
these memoranda will be selected for inclusion in the final document and some information may be used to express
the existing conditions and broad overview of opportunities in public engagement/information efforts.

EDUCATION AND TECHNOLOGY
The city has a noticeably large portion of its population with bachelor's and graduate/professional degrees. 26.8% of
the population in Fayetteville have a bachelor's degree, almost double that of the state's percentage. Furthermore,
23.3% of the population in the city has a graduate/professional degree which is three times that of Arkansas's and
twice the nation's percentage. 40% of the population is currently enrolled in some form of school, from nursery until
graduate/professional school. The percentage of people enrolled in college undergraduate or graduate school is
almost four times that of Arkansas's. 97% of households reported having a computer and 83.6% said they had an
internet subscription.

   KEY UNDERSTANDING

         · The city of Fayetteville's population is growing at a rate of 1.55%, nearly twice as fast as the
              country's, and three times that of Arkansas.

         · Fayetteville has a relatively young population:
                    o Median Age is almost 10 years less than the state's and country's median age.
                    o Percentage of people between 15 to 24 is 26%, more than double state and country.
                    o People 65 and over make up 10% of population, a far smaller percentage than the makeup
                         of the state or country.
                    o Only 17.7% of households have one or more people with a disability, a much smaller
                         percentage than the state at 32.8%.
                    o Possibly one-third of the city's population is enrolled in classes at the University.

         · Though the city is growing in diversity, it remains predominantly white:
                    o 19.8% of the population is not white; 7.5% are Black alone and 4.3% are Asian alone.
                    o 8.3% identify as Hispanic with only 5.8% identifying they speak Spanish.
                    o Only a very small percentage of the population does not speak English (0.27%)

         · The average household size is 2.18, significantly smaller Arkansas 2.47 or the national average of
              2.58. Overall, households have almost a third less children, seniors, and people with disabilities in
              them.

         · Fayetteville's demographics exemplify the college town makeup:
                    o More than a quarter of Fayetteville is currently enrolled in undergraduate and graduate
                         school and more than 40% are enrolled in some school (nursery to graduate school).
                    o More than half the population has either a Bachelor's or a higher degree; the national

WORKFORCE PROFILE
Unemployment rate in Fayetteville for 2020 was recorded at 11.7%, slightly higher than Arkansas but a little lower
than the national average. A large portion of the city's employment is in the services industry, 60.7% compared to
the state's 44.6%. 68.1% of employments are reported as white collar, higher than Arkansas's 55.2%.
Management/Business/Financial and Professional occupations also have relatively higher rates than the state's or
nation's. Major employers according to the Fayetteville Chamber of Commerce are the University of Arkansas, Tyson
Foods Inc. Wal-Mart, Springdale School District, J.B. Hunt Transport Services, Superior Industries manufacturing, as
well as the three regional major health-care providers/hospital.

Another important point of data for evaluating equity in park distribution comes from the Center for Disease
Control's (CDC) Social Vulnerability Index. The CDC assembles composite data to document levels of vulnerability for
populations at the census-tract level. The index uses 15 variables that are defined by the U.S. Census. Although the

                                                                                                                                          13
index was developed to assist in disaster planning, the criteria used to determine vulnerable populations is relevant
for the Parks and Recreation Master Plan in that it can indicate an at-risk population and census tracts that
represent a population that may be more vulnerable to both episodic and ongoing social or economic disruptions;
disaggregating the criteria in the index can assist efforts to tailor improvements to meet the needs of specific
vulnerable populations. Four themes and social factors are used to generate the index listed below. Figure 29 shows
the census tracks in the center of the city and a swath north to south that have the greatest concentrations of more
vulnerable populations.

TAPESTRY
Tapestry Segmentation classifies neighborhoods into 67 unique segments based not only on demographics but also
socioeconomic characteristics. It describes US neighborhoods in easy-to-visualize terms, ranging from Soccer Moms
to Heartland Communities. These can help in understanding customers' lifestyle choices, what they buy, and how
they spend their free time. The top 3 Tapestry segments for Fayetteville are "College Towns", "Young and Restless",
and "In Style". These are profoundly different that the state's top 3. "Rooted Rural", "Southern Satellites", and
"Middleburg", which shows the uniqueness of Fayetteville's composition and dynamics. For more information in
Tapestry Data and an explanation of segmentation visit ESRIs website at Tapestry (esri.com) and tapestry-
segmentation.pdf (esri.com)

  KEY UNDERSTANDINGS

        · Fayetteville and Arkansas's unemployment rates are slightly lower than the nations.
        · While Arkansas has a significantly larger percentage of its employees in blue collar occupations,

             Fayetteville has a noticeably larger white collar employment make up.
                  o While the national percentage of white collar employees is 61.8% and 15.2% for blue collar;
                        Fayetteville's is respectively 68.1% by 12.9% and Arkansas' is 55.2% by 27.9%.

        · Median Household Incomes in Fayetteville and Arkansas are about 25% less than that of the
             country's. Fayetteville's expected growth in income over the next five years is almost half of
             America's.
                  o This data is likely skewed due to high percentage of students.
                  o As more than 18.2% of households are making less than $15,000; compared to the state's
                        14.1% and the nation's 10.30%

        · A significant percentage of workers in Fayetteville reside within the county and means of
             communication are less reliant on cars.
                  o 84.3% of Fayetteville employees work in their county of residence, higher percentage that
                        the state or nations (74.7% and 72.3%)
                  o Compared to the state's large percentage of workers who drive alone to work (82.8%);
                        Fayetteville has a large number of workers use public transportation (1.4% compared to
                        Arkansas's 0.4%), people who bike to work (1.2% comparted to 0.2%), and walk to work (4%
                        compared to 1.7%).

        · Fayetteville's At-Risk Population should be significantly lower than the state's and nations. Asides
             from the higher percentage of "Households Below the Poverty Level" which can be neglected due to
             the status of students' income, Fayetteville has mostly half or less of the state or nation's make up in
             the other at-risk criteria.

Efforts Memorandum which are organized by year from most recent to oldest:

plan, publication year, and takeaways. This information is important to understanding the current
framework in place related to planning in the County and will be the beginning of Design

         Summary:      Adopted Jan 21st, 2020

                       Fayetteville is growing rapidly, the comprehensive plan provides a framework for
                       growth while maintaining sense of place and culture. Key objectives are infill
                       development and attainable housing. The document maintains the 6 goals from
                       the 2030 Plan, but updates the strategies to attain them.

      Big Picture  · Since the adoption of City Plan 2030, the City has seen the impact of the ...
Trends/Outlook:         aging commercial development along Martin Luther King Boulevard began to
                        redevelop, new residential subdivisions were required to provide street
                        connectivity to surrounding properties, infill development increased, and
                        redevelopment of surface parking lots were encouraged. Dense residential
                        multi-family dwellings have been constructed in Fayetteville's core and more
                        impressively in the uptown area. Active transportation systems such as the
                        trail network were planned, designed and constructed, and vast natural areas
                        and parks areas were purchased and developed. The adoption of this plan,
                        City Plan 2040, will seek to advance the progress made in the last two
                        decades. (Page 58)

                   · Fayetteville, with 37 percent of the total population of Washington County, has
                        traditionally served as the governmental, economic, and cultural center of the
                        area.

                   · For the first time the resident population of the NWA MSA increased to over
                        500,000 people with an estimated regional population of 525,032 people in
                        2016 per the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey.

                   · (The University) represents a 37 percent increase in enrollment over this 13-
                        year period. As the student population increased, so have the number of
                        faculty and staff needed to support the University's growth. This has been a
                        major driver of the population increases the City of Fayetteville has
                        experienced over the last decade.

                   · Fayetteville's median age of 27 can be largely attributed to the presence of
                        the University of Arkansas with Arkansas' median age at 37.7.

                   · Geological Data: The City of Fayetteville is located on the northwestern edge
                        of the Boston Mountains along the southeastern rim of the Springfield Plateau
                        with elevations ranging from 1,100 to 1,500 feet above sea level. (Page 86)

                   · Slopes: Of the 58,037 acres of land within the City and its' Planning Area,
                        approximately 16%, or 8,900 acres have slopes of 15 percent or greater.
                        (Page 90)

                   · Flooding: As with many municipalities, Fayetteville has challenges regarding
                        flooding throughout our community. These challenges include, but are not
                        limited to, public safety, public and private property damage and access for
                        emergency services during flood events.

                   Vision: In 2040, Fayetteville will be a resource-efficient community, in which
                   citizens and stakeholders can live, work, learn, and grow, Fayetteville will have
                   adopted policies to achieve sustainability, to provide economic growth, to
                   preserve and protect our natural and cultural resources, and to enhance the
                   quality of life for all residents. Residents will have equitable access to
                   neighborhoods that are healthy, walkable, and distinct. (page 21) Goals:

                     Specific Objectives Related to Parks and Open Space:

                     · 3.1.5 Reinvest in parks, streets, and civic buildings within the heart of
                          the city. The tree-lined streets, parks, and historic civic buildings found in
                          Fayetteville's older neighborhoods greatly contribute to the unique community
                          character and high quality of life that residents treasure. Preservation of our
                          tree-lined streets and parks and adaptive reuse of our historic civic buildings
                          will maintain the community cultural identity. The City should continue to
                          utilize the Enduring Green Network map to identify and preserve high-value
                          open spaces that help

                     · 3.3.3 Increase the viability of businesses by leveraging the economic
                          performance of appealing environments that are mixed-use, walkable,
                          and integrated with green space. to create an interconnected green
                          network throughout the community. The Razorback Regional Greenway
                          illustrates the ability of the City to leverage capital investments in trail
                          infrastructure to drive economic development. began building the Scull Creek
                          Trail with $2.1 million in funding provided by a bond issue passage. Additional
                          yearly Capital Improvement Project funding of $1.3 million annually was used
                          to build-out the remainder of the trail. The economic development catalyst that
                          the trail provided is evidenced by the residential and commercial development
                          occurring in nodes along the trail spine in south Fayetteville, throughout
                          downtown/Dickson Street, in mid-town around Poplar Street, and throughout
                          the uptown district along Mud Creek.

                     · 3.4.9 Expand and interconnect the sidewalk and trail system at the
                          neighborhood, citywide, and regional levels. The trail network has
                          expanded by 14.5 linear miles of new trail since the adoption of City Plan
                          2030 in 2011. Major trail projects completed in this time frame include
                          connecting Kessler Mountain Park and the completion of the Niokaski Trail.
                          Trail projects currently underway include the extension of the Mud Creek Trail
                          to Gulley Park, Clabber Creek Trail and the St. Paul Trail in Southeast
                          Fayetteville. Numerous short trail segments are also included in the Trail 5-
                          year Plan to close gaps.

                     · 3.5.1 Vigilantly nurture a continuum of greenspace, including

· 3.5.2 Strategically plan for and acquire land that can be incorporated
     into the Enduring Green Network. A network of these smaller open spaces
     within walking distance of all residents provides both environmental services
     and benefits to the mental and physical health of residents in surrounding
     neighborhoods that may not have access to larger, regional parks. The City's
     ability to recognize and acquire important green spaces, both large and small,
     is essential for building a vibrant and healthy city.

· 3.5.3 Promote conservation easements and alternative development
     patterns that encourage efficient use of land.

Natural Areas consist of lands approximating or reverting to a wilderness
conditions, including those with limited development potential due to topography,
hydrology, vegetation or value as an environmental resource. These resources
can include stream and wildlife corridors, as well as natural hubs and cores, many
of which are identified in the generalized enduring green network. A Natural Area
designation would encourage a development pattern that requires conservation
and preservation, prevents degradation of these areas, and would utilize the
principles of low impact development stormwater infrastructure for all
developments. Natural Areas are prime candidates for conservation subdivision
design and/or clustered development patterns. The guiding policies for Natural
Areas are:
1.Preserve a network of habitat and open space, thereby protecting biodiversity
and enhancing the City's quality of life.
2.Preserve native vegetation and meet the habitat needs of multiple species.
3.Encourage recreational and educational opportunities in appropriate areas to
enhance appreciation of existing environmental resources.
4.Identify areas of environmental concern and protect and preserve environmental
resources.
5.Conserve open space and protect areas of significant riparian benefit, tree
canopy and other environmental resource through cluster development
provisions, density controls, protective easements and/or other development
tools.

Civic and Private Open Space/Parklands are sites that are permanently dedicated
to open space or parkland. Fayetteville is fortunate to have abundant parklands
well positioned geographically across and throughout the City. Publicly accessible
open space is essential for residents to have convenient access to outdoor
amenities. Public open spaces can also serve as catalytic economic development
opportunities to lure visitors to the City for special events. This is evident in the
amount of use that the City has experienced with our many local multi-purpose
paved trails and the increasing number of mountain bike facilities
that have been constructed in our public parks. Additionally, the realization of the
Kessler Mountain Regional Park has brought in many visitors to participate in
local and regional sporting events. As the City fills in with new development the

         Plan Title:
Publication Year:          Master Streets Plan
         Summary:          Update with 2040 Plan

                           The Master Street Plan is a policy document to help guide decisions regarding
                           location, form, function, design, and classifications of streets. The Plan considers
                           infrastructure and anticipates where new building developments might occur to
                           plan for possible street connections and capital expenditures. Existing and
                           projected conditions, such as population growth, economic conditions, land use,
                           natural and cultural resources, etc. are taken into consideration to imagine what a
                           city might look like decades in the future. Master Street Plans include maps and
                           designs ­ showing the location of current and suggested future streets, as well as
                           potential designs of a roadway.

                           near Lake Fayetteville on the north and MLK Boulevard on the south. In addition,
                           the Mud Creek and Town Branch Trails connect the Greenway to 71B. Aparallel
                           bikeway system is developing east of College Avenue along Old Missouri Road
                           and Old Wire Road. A future trail along Sublett Creek will run from Mission and
                           North to College and Poplar. (Page 21)

                           corridor, and upgraded that service in 2019 with more frequent headways.

                     Avenue and to a lesser degree South School Avenue. This provides alternative
                     routes for local circulation, helping to reduce congestion, traffic conflicts, and
                     potentially crashes along the street and at major intersections.
                     ·Managing access along the corridor and reducing the number of driveway cuts
                     and turning conflicts. Techniques to retain good local access include building
                     alternative routes, providing more public street intersections to replace curb cuts
                     and improve user orientation, and establishing shared access points with better
                     interconnections among existing parking lots and driveways.
                     ·Modifying street sections along 71B itself to improve pedestrian and in some
                     cases bicycle access, calming traffic where needed, and "right-sizing" segments
                     of the corridor to be more consistent with actual traffic volume.
                     ·Improving major points of congestion and clusters of crashes.
                     ·Improving pedestrian and bicycle crossings of the corridor.
                     ·Developing a parallel shared use path system that provided access to most of
                     the corridor's present and future destinations and connects to the regional trail
                     system, including the Razorback Greenway and the planned Sublett Creek Trail.

                     regional bus rapid transit (BRT) line with specific station stops.

              Entity:   City of Fayetteville,
         Plan Title:
Publication Year:       Cultural Arts Corridor
         Summary:       2017-Ongoing

                        The Cultural Arts Corridor is a dynamic new 50-acre outdoor public space that will
                        help to revitalize Fayetteville's downtown area and create a destination for
                        residents and visitors alike. Linking the City's key cultural institutions--including
                        the Walton Arts Center, Theatre Squared, Nadine Baum Studios, Fayetteville
                        Public Library, and the University of Arkansas' Art and Design District--the
                        corridor will showcase and celebrate local arts culture. It will also enhance civic
                        space and serve as a catalyst for additional development and density in the
                        downtown area, increasing bike trails and connections, and improving streets and
                        walkability. This project is part of a Bond package approved by Fayetteville voters
                        in April 2019.

                         This plan takes an in-depth look at how we can build on our small, everyday
                         actions to make the biggest positive impact on both Fayetteville and the globe.

                         This plan is a guide to reducing waste, reducing our energy use, and moving to

                         cleaner and more sustainable types of energy. The City believes that this plan will

                         lay the groundwork for a thriving, beautiful community for generations to come.

     · Creating a Downtown Park
The Center Prairie Trail is identified as a priority in the Fayetteville Alternative
Transportation and Trail Master Plan developed by the City of Fayetteville in
association with the Sidewalk and Trails Committee and citizens in 2003. An
opportunity exists for a large park Downtown, approximately 6 acres in size along
the Scull Creek and the proposed Center Prairie Trail walking and bike trail. The
majority of the land is currently owned by noted architect Fay Jones. A priority
action for the City is to negotiate with Mr. Jones to acquire the property for this
important civic purpose.
The character of the park should not change drastically from its current condition,
acting as a passive recreational park. The proposed Center Prairie Trail will form
a central spine through the park. Additional walking trails can be installed to
connect Mountain Street to West Street and to the Blair Library. A landscape
architect will need to be employed to create a detailed plan of the park. The park
designers will need to assess each exist-ing tree as to its value. Invasive species
of plants should be removed. The detailed plan may call for additional clearing of
the understory to enhance views through the park, and to take advantage of key
geographic features.
Security for visitors to the park is a concern that will need to be incorporated into
the detailed design. Neighboring houses should face the park with windows to
provide natural surveillance. The City should assess whether or not the park

             City of Fayetteville, AK  Parks System Master Plan Existing Plans Memo
                                                                               Page 32 of 39
                              should be closed after sunset. Lighting and security cameras should also be
                              considered for the park's crime prevention program.

                              Mid Term:

                                   · Enhancing the Downtown Square: The Downtown Square is the historic
                                         center of Fayetteville. It is where some of the first businesses were
                                         established in town. The Old Post Office is located in the center of the
                                         square. Scheduled events and activities make the Downtown Square a
                                         gathering place for the community. The plan calls for preserving the
                                         historic buildings surrounding the Square and encouraging infill
                                         development where appropriate. A mix of uses would continue to
                                         enhance and activate the Square. The plan recommends maintaining
                                         diagonal parking along the Square and illustrates possible locations for
                                         nearby parking structures convenient to the Square. The parking decks
                                         would be lined with habitable space or be located behind existing
                                         structures. In addition to mechanisms to alleviate parking needs, the
                                         plan also encourages pedestrian friendly streets around and adjacent to
                                         the Square. Walkable streets would allow Downtown residents and
                                         visitors easy access to the Square, and allow for convenient connections
                                         to other areas of Downtown, including Dickson Street and the Fayetteville
                                         Public Library (Blair Library).

                       City of Fayetteville, AK     Parks System Master Plan Existing Plans Memo

Summary:                   The Walker Park Neighborhood embodies significant portions of Fayetteville's
                           history as one of the oldest neighborhoods in the City and former home to notable
                           Fay-etteville and Arkansas figures such as Archibald Yell. Changes over time have
                           shaped the neighborhood's development pattern as the area shifted from a
                           predominantly rural area to a modest extension of downtown neighborhoods to an
                           area zoned for multi-family housing. Development pressure is inevitable given the
                           area's proximity to Downtown and the Arkansas Research and Technology Park.
                           Planning enables stakeholders to influence the form of future development by
                           setting forth a vision document that encourages traditional neighborhood
                           development and sustainability.

    Plan Strategies        Guiding Principles
                    and
                           1.  Balance of Uses and Housing
Recommendations
                        :  2.  Connectivity and Walkability

                           3.  Jefferson Square as Neighborhood Core

                           4.  Accessible Greenspace

                           Walker Park

                           Walker Park serves as a key destination for neighborhood residents, containing

                           multiple ball fields, playgrounds, the Fayetteville Senior Center, the City's only

                           skate park and a BMX track. Adding uses and expanding the Park's trail access

                           will lead to increased Park usage from neighbor-hood and City residents.

                                                                    Walker Park currently functions as a barrier
                                                                    between the businesses on South School Avenue
                                                                    and the residents of the neighborhood. A system of
                                                                    paved and natural trails throughout the park would
                                                                    enable residents to access the business
                                                                    establishments without having to drive. The location
                                                                    of Spout Spring Creek along the western side of the
                                                                    park in particular prohibits the connection between
                                                                    the park and the South School corridor. The
                                                                    illustrative plan envisions a number of new linkages
                                                                    along the western bound-ary of the park. On-street
                                                                    linkages would be developed by extensions of 9th
                                                                    Street and 13th Street, connecting the park to
                                                                    South School Avenue. These street extensions
                                                                    would provide pedestrian access on sidewalks
                                                                    adjacent to the new street extensions. Additionally,
                                                                    a dedicated trail connection is shown at the 9th
                                                                    Street intersection, linking Walker Park to the Frisco
                                                                    Trail corridor. The pedestrian linkages to the
                           neighborhoods west of South School Avenue are vital to encouraging the broader
                           neighborhood's use of this open space resource.

                       The Walker Park neighborhood plan offers some suggestions for Park
                       improvements that align with community values including a dog park, disk golf
                       course, natural areas restoration and wildflower meadows and a small
                       amphitheater. Increasing trails, pedestrian, and vehicle connections into and
                       around the park as well as how the neighborhood streets promote park connection.

MEMORANDUM PURPOSE

This memo is intended to summarize the current programs and recreation facilities offered through Fayetteville,
analyze trends, and identify potential gaps. The memo is based on information provided by the City of Fayetteville,
on workshops held by the project team, and by information available on the City's website. Key information from
this memo may be included in the final document, and some of the information may be used to express existing
conditions and a broad overview of opportunities in public engagement / information efforts.

This report addresses the following:

     · Current State of Recreation Programming
     · Current Recreation Service Offerings
     · Recreation Programming Trends
     · Gap Analysis
     · Program Services Challenges and Opportunities

CURRENT STATE OF RECREATION PROGRAMMING

Introduction
With a mission to "meet the needs of all by providing a safe and diversified park system that encourages community
pride, visionary planning and operations, and environmental stewardship", the City of Fayetteville supports
recreation for its residents and visitors in a variety of ways through parks and open space providing space for active
and passive recreation offerings. Some of the recreational offerings include picnic areas, biking and mountain biking
trails, playgrounds, basketball, volleyball, horseshoes, disc golf, softball, boating, fishing, and many more. Residents
and visitors can enjoy over 80 miles of natural surface trails and boardwalks, 27 playgrounds, 7 tennis courts, 7
volleyball courts, 3 lakes, a swimming pool, new splashpad, skate park, plus many more recreational opportunities.
The City's Parks and Recreation Department hosts a plethora of events most notable being the Gulley Park Summer
Concert Series and the Homegrown Music Festival at Kessler Mountain. Mountain bike trails are also becoming a
popular venue for mountain biking events.1

Fayetteville Recreation Department
Recreation services are offered by the City of Fayetteville through their Parks and Recreation Department. The
Recreation division consists of seven full time staff supplemented by 5.62 FTEs of part-time and seasonal staff. Staff
is relatively young but skilled. Staff are further supported by a large contingent of volunteers. (In 2019, volunteer
coaches provided nearly 233,000 hours between youth soccer, baseball, and fast pitch softball.) The Department's
budget allocated for 2021 is approximately $5.4M including both the General Fund and Parks Development Fund.
CURRENT RECREATION SERVICE OFFERINGS

A variety of recreational services are provided in Fayetteville through parks and open spaces, recreational facilities,
and recreational programming.

Fayetteville Properties
The City of Fayetteville manages over 4,000 acres of public parkland, including 5 regional parks, 5 community parks,
over 30 neighborhood parks and special interest areas, 8 natural areas, and 15 Greenways and trail corridors that
connect parks and other destinations throughout the city.2 The types of recreational offerings at each of the
properties is listed in Figure 1 below.

Recreational Program Offerings
The City of Fayetteville provides a variety of recreational programming. Adult, youth, aquatic, community, and race
series are some of the types of events offered. Many community programs are offered at the Yvonne Richardson
Community Center (YRCC), while aquatic programs are typically offered at dedicated facilities. Numerous recreation
programs were cancelled, shortened, or altered in 2020 and early 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Some of the most popular programs based on attendance numbers and programs that typically have waitlists
include the following:

     · Adult softball
                                                                                                                                           3

Program Services Inventory and Assessment (Task 1.6) Draft
     · Be Active! summer camps
     · Swim lessons
     · Youth soccer (younger ages)
     · YRCC summery camp
     · YRCC Kids Nite (after school program)

In response to input from focus groups and the general popularity of outdoor recreation (hiking, camping, etc.) in
this region of Arkansas, the City recently started the "Outdoor Fayetteville" program which features a series of
outdoor trips and recreation opportunities with equipment provided. Attendance has so far been limited, but the
program is new and was impacted in its first years by COVID.

Other programs that currently see limited attendance include Fast Pitch Softball, Movies in the Park/Dive-In Movies,
the Adult Soccer League, and Kessler Mt. Jam (mountain bike event).

Recreational Facilities
City recreation programs are hosted at City-owned recreation facilities that encompass a combination of indoor and
outdoor structures, parks, and pools.

As of the time of this memo, the City manages approximately 27,800 sf of indoor recreation structures and
approximately 18,290 sf of outdoor recreation structures. Indoor recreation structures represent recreation sheds,
the Fayetteville Senior Center, the YRCC, and the Wilson Park pool facility. Outdoor recreation structures represent
facilities such as docks, piers, and recreation open air shelters and not ball fields, lakes, etc. that are included in the
overall park acreages. The average age of the structures is 17 years old (if counting from the most recent renovation
of Wilson Park Pool) or 23 years (if counting from the date the structures were built).

Approximately 51 courts and paved recreation facilities ­ representing 150,000 sf ­ are managed by the City. All
court facilities are older, with some courts built in the 1980s and 1990s. The courts in Wilson Park have seen the
most recent renovations. Non-court facilities included in this category are batting cages, horseshoes, and the Walker
Skate Park.

The City also manages several turf fields. Fields include softball, baseball, soccer, disc golf, with artificial turf fields
installed in 2019 and 2020 at Gary Hampton Softball Complex and Kessler Mountain Regional Park, respectively.

Lastly, the City is responsible for two water recreation amenities ­ the Wilson Park Pool and the Walker Park Splash
Pad. The pool is an older facility with recent renovations, while the splash pad is new (installed 2019).

Recreation Partners
Local partners also contribute to recreational offerings with the City of Fayetteville. Such partners include:

     · Ozark Botanical Gardens
     · Boys & Girls Club
     · Horseshoe Association
     · Ozark Flyers Club
     · Ozark Volleyball Club
     · Public School Partnership
     · Rowing Club
     · Senior Activity & Wellness Center
     · Friends of the YRCC
     · Fayetteville Youth Baseball
     · Arkansas Hawks
     · Fayetteville Disc Golf
     · Fayetteville Disc Association (Ultimate Frisbee)

Program Services Inventory and Assessment (Task 1.6) Draft
Note that the Friends of the YRCC (Yvonne Richardson Community Center) do not directly provide programming;
rather they fundraise to cover program expenses at the YRCC, which are run by the City internally.
The City contracts with the swim coach of the Razorback Aquatics Club for the City's internal recreation swim team.
The University offers its own recreational opportunities to students, staff, and faculty who may live within or around
Fayetteville. While not analyzed in this memo, the University's offerings and the University population should be
considered when planning the future growth of recreation programs by the City.

RECREATION PROGRAMMING TRENDS

National Trends in Parks and Recreation
Please refer to Memo 1.4 for a thorough look into national recreation trends, including trends in general fitness,
individual and team sports, outdoor recreation, and youth sports. Upcoming hot topics that may apply to
Fayetteville include climate change impacts, technology, and pets.

Arkansas and Fayetteville Activity Trends
Please refer to Memo 1.4 for a closer examination of activity trends in Arkansas and the Fayetteville area. In general,
residents of Fayetteville are recreating more than the average American, with tennis, ice skating, soccer, frisbee,
and Pilates indicated as activities significantly more popular in Fayetteville than the national average.

GAP ANALYSIS

Recreation Facility Analysis
One way to examine how the City is currently serving its current population and anticipate growth needs is to
examine the number of recreational facilities provided compared to the population. The National Recreation and
Parks Association (NRPA) collects metrics from park and recreation agencies around the country to develop an
annual Agency Performance Review. The tables below show Fayetteville's current population per facility compared
to the national average across all agencies, as well as to agencies in similar categories to Fayetteville. These similar
categories and why they were chosen include:

     · Jurisdiction population of 50,000 to 99,999 ­ Fayetteville's current population is within this range
     · Jurisdiction population of 100,000 to 250,000 ­ Fayetteville's projected 2040 population is within this range
     · Acres maintained of over 3,500 ­ the City has over 4,000 acres of publicly accessible natural areas, parks,

          and greenways/trail corridors
     · Southwest Region ­ the NRPA region including Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Texas

Program Services Inventory and Assessment (Task 1.6) Draft
RECREATION PROGRAM SERVICES CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES

Potential Challenges
Based on the above inventory and analysis, some major challenges for recreation program services include upkeep
of aging facilities, recovering from the impact on attendance from COVID, and an overall trend in decreasing
program attendance. Other challenges noted in the stakeholder meetings included: finding an appropriate balance
between recreation and competition for youth sports; maxed out and older facilities; desire for more staff and
marketing; and a lack of lighting at some outdoor facilities. It is also important to remember that there are a finite
number of children with a finite amount of time in Fayetteville ­ too many program offerings may result in low
attendance numbers simply due to the dilution of kids across programs. Looking to the future, building or expanding
facilities to meet the demand of an increasing and evolving population, as well as hiring the staff needed to operate
and maintain them, may become a challenge depending on the financial outlook of the City budgets.

Opportunities and Considerations
The City has much potential for expanding, refining, and strengthening their recreation service offerings to meet the
needs of the community now and into the future. The rest of this memo explores opportunities for how this may be
done, as well as several considerations that should be kept in mind as the Master Plan develops and makes
recommendations for the parks and recreation system.

As a whole, it will be critical to consider how recreational facilities and program offerings will best keep pace with
both the increasing population and changing demographics. Building flexibility into future facilities ­ both in terms
of being flexible for the types of recreation programs that can be offered and in terms of accommodating revenue
generating opportunities such as rentals and concessions ­ will help the City be adaptable and address changes in
recreation trends and popular programs over time. For all facilities, the City should continue to support and
advocate for quality maintenance and timely repairs of recreation facilities, including courts and fields, to enhance
their longevity, reduce closure times, and extend the time needed between renovations and replacements.

While COVID generally negatively impacted recreation, it can also be used as a source of inspiration. Embrace
lessons learned during the COVID-19 pandemic and consider how virtual or hybrid programs or volunteer training
may integrate into future service offerings. While this may not be realistic for all types of programs, race series and
concert series may be particularly suitable; for example, virtual race series or livestreamed concerts. Providing more
virtual opportunities for training volunteers can help strengthen and expand the City's already strong volunteer
coaching program.

The City can also build upon its existing partner network. Look to existing or new partners to provide additional
recreation services different from what the City provides, or to take over providing programs that see low
attendance and may be better served by an outside provider. Regular evaluation of programs offered by the City can
reveal which programs may be candidates for discontinuation with transition to a local partner. The City can also
explore new partnerships to help fund/sponsor new or expanded recreation programs.

                                                                                     1 | Draft Community Engagement Summary
The purpose of this document is to share community
comments and feedback that help inform the next
steps in the Parks and Recreation Master Plan
process. The Fayetteville Park System Master Plan
Community Vision Workshop held two Community
Values Meetings and an online survey managed
through the City's Speak Up page. The Community
Values Meetings took place on Saturday, February 19,
2022, from 10:00- noon at Veterans Memorial Park
and from 2:00-4:00 pm at Centennial Park.

This document is organized into the following sections:
    1) Engagement Summary Overview
    2) Online Survey Key Findings
    3) Mapping Activity Key Findings
    4) Visual Preference Dot Activity Key Findings
    5) Additional City Surveys

SECTION 1: ENGAGEMENT SUMMARY OVERVIEW

Overall Trends and Themes
· In general, respondents would like to see more gathering places and sense of community in

    parks, more trails and connections and waterplay in parks.
· Comments prioritize increase water recreation, specifically natural swimming and water quality,

    at Lake Fayetteville, Lake Sequoya, and Lake Wilson.
· There is a desire for new parks, noting gaps on the west side of the city.
· Accessibility and amenities open to the public is important.
· There is more interest in more outdoor sports courts than indoor facilities.
· Comments indicate a desire for increased hangout places like food, bars, event spaces near

    and around parks.
· Wayfinding and nature education could be included in all parks.

Engagement Conclusions and Alignment with 2021 Community wide Survey
Based on the results of this survey and when compared to the findings from the 2021 community-
wide survey, which was the foundation of the concepts presented to the community, the following
conclusions can be made to drive the next phases of the plan.

Demographics- Key Findings
Participation. 58 total community members attended the in-person workshops, and 550
responded to the online survey. Of both meetings, nearly 50% of attendees were between the
ages of 25 and 45. The in-person meetings attracted more responses from younger (under 18)
and older (55+) demographics. Based on the community profile of Fayetteville, where the median
age is 29.2, there is a slight skew to this middle age bracket. It could be assumed that the 25-45
age group responses advocate for younger household members (under 18). Additional

                                                                                    2 | Draft Community Engagement Summary
engagement could explore targeting the 18-24 age group, which is traditionally difficult to engage.
All four wards are equally represented in the survey, ranging from 22-25% in each ward. The in-
person meetings had slightly more attendance from South Fayetteville residents than North
Fayetteville. Interestingly, only 22% of survey respondents had participated in the planning effort
previously, with 18% having taken the community-wide survey. The information in this document
reflects the perspectives of 475 residents new to this planning effort.

Visitation. About 80% total participants visit parks on average monthly or more. This is about 15%
higher than the community-wide survey which 64% of respondents visited parks monthly or more.
This is expected given the likelihood of participation in the planning effort to attract more frequent
park users. It can be assumed that the information in this document is more representative of
current park users desires for improvements rather than what may attract non-park users.

Themes and Goals (Survey and Dot Exercise)- Key Findings
The presentation and corresponding questions were intended to provide background context and
the opportunity for the community to provide direction on the preliminary plan goals. The five
primary plan these, the organizing structure of the presentation, survey and ultimately the plan,
were all well supported by the community. Outdoor lifestyle was most supported in the in-person
meetings and natural resource management was the most supported in the online survey. Quality
sustainable places and care ranked the lowest both in person and online, but only by a few
percentage points.

Outdoor Lifestyle. The goals most supported in outdoor lifestyle include connecting people to
water and increasing vegetation and nature in parks. The dot exercise indicated kayaking and
blue way trails and natural swimming areas as the highest ranked strategies for this goal. This is
supported by the City initiated survey on park amenities which also ranked canoe and kayak
launch as highly rated. The mapping exercise further emphasized the importance of natural
swimming areas, specifically at Lake Fayetteville and Lake Sequoyah. The community-wide survey
also ranked natural swimming areas (61%) at Lake Fayetteville and White River. Increased nature
programs ranked lower on the goals, however environmental education ranked highly on desired
amenities.

Quality, Sustainable Places and Care. Maintenance and replacement of current park amenities
ranked notably higher than any of the other goals under this theme. The dot exercise indicated
expansion to parks, inclusive parks and improvement to existing parks as the top strategies. This
aligns closely with the findings of the community-wide survey which highlights improving and
building parks in underserved areas (77%) and improve existing parks (71%) as important.

Active and Well. The goals in this theme are well balanced based on the community feedback.
Some emphasis was placed on program offerings to meet the needs of all and enhancing trail
corridors. The dot exercise indicated more support for an off-leash dog park, pickleball courts.
Dog parks also ranked highly on the by the City initiated survey on park amenities. Question 7 one
the community-wide survey indicated a desire for more pickleball, tennis, basketball courts (47%)
Question 8 on the community-wide survey also indicated a community desire for dog-parks (22%).

                                                                                     3 | Draft Community Engagement Summary
Multipurpose field were not ranked very highly on the dot exercise or on the community-wide
survey.

Gathering and Placemaking. Increasing community gathering spaces and park events were highly
supported goals. The dot exercise indicated that all the amenities would be supported, concerts
and movies, farmers markets and games received the most support. This is supported by question
3 in the community-wide survey where 91% of respondents indicated that parks are places for
people to spend time outdoors.

Natural Systems Management. The goals in this theme are well balanced based on the
community feedback. Some emphasis was placed on improving forests and waterway habitats
and increased biodiversity. The dot exercise indicated a preference for green infrastructure,
conservation efforts and restoration over natural amenities such as fishing ad birding.
Environmental education was ranked highly and corresponds to the community-wide survey
Question 7 where 72% of respondents would like to see more environmental education.

Locational Recommendations (Mapping Exercise)- Key Findings
The mapping exercise serves as an opportunity for the community to show us where some of the
goals and strategies can be geographically located. The survey and dot exercise focused on `the
what', and the mapping exercise focuses on `the where'. These activities are intended to support
one another to increase our understanding for potential plan improvements and
recommendations.

The mapping exercise further emphasized the importance of natural swimming areas, specifically
at Lake Fayetteville and Lake Sequoyah. This was also supported by the community-wide survey,
where 42% of respondents prioritized natural swimming areas. Urban camping ranked highly as
well, also supported by the community-wide survey, 73% of respondents would like to see more.

The exercise and the City initiated survey note a community preference for focusing on the
community parks and regional parks, with Lake Sequoyah, Lake Fayetteville, Underwood Park,
Walker Park, and Kessler Mountain Park receiving the most sticker comments for suggested
improvements. The improvements to these parks focus on natural swimming, water quality,
Maintenance, preservation and inclusivity, and amenities such as restrooms and parking.

This activity offered a write in option, and several suggestions were made for additional park
improvements not listed in the survey or dot exercises. There were a few suggestions for a track,
areas to increase safety and lighting, areas for improved maintenance, the inclusion of art in parks,
and increased events/food/gathering.

Critical Needs- Key Findings
The top-rated concerns for this parks plan to address include improvements to current parks
facilities and adding new amenities to existing parks. This aligned with feedback from the
Community-wide survey. In addition, access, inclusion, and mobility ranked highly, which also
scored highly in the community-wide survey as 77% thought it was essential to build parks in
underserved areas and 71% thought it was essential to improve existing parks and facilities.

                                                                                     4 | Draft Community Engagement Summary
Alignment with 2018 Survey
Feedback gathered in 2018 proves supportive of recent feedback, despite societal
changes experienced over the last few years with the pandemic. In 2018, public feedback
pointed to a community that prioritized a park system that could help constituents live a
healthy active lifestyle with many opportunities for contact with nature. Social interaction,
planning in an equitable manner, and slightly increasing the overall quality of the parks
system were priorities.

Fayetteville Parks System Master Plan Survey                              Report of Results

Executive Summary

About the Survey

The City of Fayetteville contracted with the City of Fayetteville and Design Workshop to help
complete an update of their Parks and Recreation System Master Plan. As part of this effort, Polco's
National Research Center (NRC) was engaged to conduct a representative survey of residents to
gather feedback on their use of, and preferences for, parks and recreation in the community. The
survey was developed through an iterative process with NRC, City staff and the Design Workshop
team, and was a part of a multi-faceted outreach process to gather information from the
community.

Survey Administration

To ensure a representative sample of residents, a total of 6,000 residential addresses were
randomly selected from a list of all residential addresses in Fayetteville. Each of these selected
households was contacted two times (a postcard followed by a letter) to invite them to complete
the survey online (using the provided URL). Of the 6,000 households, 729 completed the survey,
providing a response rate of 12%. A typical response rate for this type of survey ranges from 5% to
15%. The margin of error for this Address-Sampled survey with 729 respondents is ±3.6%.

Additionally, the City made concerted efforts to invite all residents to complete an Open
Participation version of the survey. All questions were the same, but the data collection was kept
separate so that results from the Address-Sample and the Open Participation efforts could be
compared (see Error! Reference source not found.Error! Reference source not found.). The City
was successful in their outreach efforts and 935 responded to the Open Participation survey.

Overall, respondents to the Open Participation effort were more likely than respondents to the
Address-Sampled survey to be active users of the parks system.

The survey data from both efforts were statistically weighted to adjust for under-response that
commonly occurs among certain demographic groups, a survey research best practice. While
renters, those in attached housing units and younger adults (18-34) did not respond in proportions
equal to their census demographics, responses to the Address-Sampled survey were received from
205 renters, 160 attached-housing dwellers and 140 younger adults. These numbers are robust for
the representation of these three groups and their responses were weighted to match the Census
proportions to ensure their correct level of representation in the overall results. Comparisons of
results by respondent characteristics and geographic area of residence are reported in Appendices
D to H. More information about the survey methods, including weighting, can be found in Error!
Reference source not found..

The results of the Open Participation are compared to those of the random address sample in
Error! Reference source not found. and the detailed frequencies are provided in Appendices B and
C.

Key Findings

Most people in Fayetteville used parks at least a few times a year.
       · Approximately 64% of residents used a park, playground, or picnic area weekly or
            monthly and approximately 69% have used trails and natural areas weekly or monthly
            (see Error! Reference source not found.).

       · About 64% of respondents reported attending events such as Gulley Concerts or running
            and cycling races at least a few times a year.

       · About half had used sports fields or courts, and about two-thirds has attended events such
            as Gulley concerts or running/cycling races.

       · Close to 80% had never participated in sports leagues, while about 70% had not used a
            swimming pool or recreation center.

Residents felt that parks and recreation facilities and programs should be
provided for a variety of purposes, but top was providing a beautiful place to
enjoy outdoors.

       · About 90% of households strongly agreed that the top three purposes the City should
            provide parks were 1) places for people to spend time outdoors in nature, 2) to contribute
            to a more beautiful community and to 3) provide places for all to play (see Error!
            Reference source not found.). Protecting the natural environment and promoting
            environmental sustainability followed closely behind these three purposes.

Not knowing what was available or where to go, was top of list for potential
problems encountered using Fayetteville parks, recreation facilities, community
centers or programs.

       · Forty-five percent of those with an opinion said insufficient information was a major or
            moderate problem for use of parks, recreation facilities, community centers or programs
            (see Error! Reference source not found.).

       · Lack of parking was not a concern to about 40% of respondents (19% reported parks as
            too crowded as a moderate or major problem and 22% reported lack of parking as a
            moderate or major problem)

       · Roughly half of respondents felt parks were convenient to get to and were close enough
            for them to bike or bike to, however, less than 20 percent thought convenience and
            closeness was a major or moderate problem. A larger percentage from the Open
            Participation survey indicated distance or ease of access to parks to be problem.

       · Park safety and maintenance were not considered a problem to more than half of
            respondents (55%) and considered a minor or moderate problem to a third of
            respondents. Open Participation survey respondents were twice as likely to think these
            items were a problem.

2955 Valmont Road, Suite 300; Boulder, CO 80301  303-444-7863  n-r-c.com
Fayetteville Parks System Master Plan Survey                              Report of Results

Overall, residents prefer more passive, nature-based activities to competitive and
organized sports.

       · Most residents (83%) thought there should be more community gardens. (The 83%
            includes the category

       · About three-quarters also thought there were too few community `Hangouts' with yard
            games, places for urban camping and environmental education/nature centers (see
            Error! Reference source not found.).

       · Asked to choose the top 4 facilities, places or programs to prioritize for development in
            the next 10 years, these were cited by 20% or more:

              o Community gardens where residents can grow vegetables and flowers, 29%

              o Designated areas for natural environment preservation/conservation and open
                   space, 25%

              o City-maintained gardens such as the square and Wilson Park, 23%

              o Places for off-leash dogs to play or exercise, 22%

              o Playgrounds, 22%

              o Open space and natural areas, 21%

              o Water recreation (e.g., kayaking, fishing, canoeing, etc.), 20%

       · Lowest priority were recreation equipment rentals, competitive sports leagues and
            softball/baseball fields.

Natural swimming areas were of more interest than pools.
       · If the City were to invest in new swimming facilities, most residents (61%) would prefer
            to see the City improve water quality at Lake Fayetteville. (See Error! Reference source
            not found.)

       · About 4 in 10 would prefer investment in a natural swimming hole at White River or an
            outdoor water park with slides and lazy river center.

       · Development of indoor pools were preferred by closer to one-quarter to two-thirds of
            respondents.

Supporting the environment and conserving and connecting natural areas were
seen as the most important focuses for Fayetteville in the coming years.

       · A strong majority of residents thought it was essential or very important to:

              o Design or improve parks to support the environment (e.g., reduce flooding, improve
                   air and water quality, etc.), 80%

              o Preserve and connect more natural areas, 80%

              o Improve or build parks in underserved areas of the city, 77%

       · Most also thought it was essential or very important to:

              o Acquire additional land to protect and preserve undeveloped open space in the city,
                   72%

2955 Valmont Road, Suite 300; Boulder, CO 80301  303-444-7863  n-r-c.com

              o Improve existing parks and facilities, 71%.

       · Lowest as a community priority were building a new indoor recreation center or
            designing or improving parks where people can play sports, but about 4 in 10 were
            interested in these. (See Error! Reference source not found.)

Asked to rank six actions the City could take in the next five years, improving
access and enhancing current resources were top of the list.

       · About half of respondents put completing undeveloped parks to improve park access and
            connectivity and focusing on projects that renovate/enhance existing parks and natural
            areas in the top two priorities (see Error! Reference source not found. ).

       · Third in importance was expanding by acquiring new property for future parks and
            natural lands.

       · Lower ranked was seeking additional funding for park facilities, increasing resources for
            recreation program and community facilities offerings and increasing resources devoted
            to maintenance

Appendix A: Comparisons of Address Sample and Open
Participation Survey Responses (Excluding "Don't know" or "Not
applicable")

Understanding the Tables

For ease of comparison between subgroups, the questions show summarized responses for only the proportion of respondents giving a
positive answer; for example, the percent of respondents who "strongly or somewhat agreed" or gave a rating of "very or somewhat
positive" or "more favorable". Those who chose "Don't know" or "Not applicable" are not included in the percentages ­ it is the percent of
respondents "with an opinion."

The subgroup comparison tables contain the crosstabulations of responses to the random address survey by responses to the Open
Participation survey. Chi-square or ANOVA tests of significance were applied to these breakdowns of survey questions. A "p-value" of 0.05
or less indicates that there is less than a 5% probability that differences observed between groups are due to chance; or in other words, a
greater than 95% probability that the differences observed in the selected categories of the sample represent "real" differences among
those populations. As subgroups vary in size and each group has a unique margin of error, statistical testing is used to determine whether
differences between subgroups are statistically significant.

Each column in the following tables is labeled with a letter for each subgroup being compared. The letters start over with "A" for each
different characteristic. (For example, in Table 1: Question 2 by Outreach Type, the Address Sample respondents are marked "A" and Open
Participation respondents are marked "B"; whereas in Table 57: Question 2 by Tenure, Length of Residency and Housing Type (Address
Sample) for housing tenure, renters and owners are marked "A" and "B", and then for type of housing unit, those in single family are
marked "A" and other homes are marked "B".)

For each pair of subgroup ratings within a characteristic within a row that has a statistically significant difference, an uppercase letter
denoting significance is shown in the cell with the larger column proportion. The letter denotes the subgroup with the smaller column
proportion from which it is statistically different. Cells have also been shaded grey when there were statistically significant differences
between the address sample survey and the Open Participation survey responses. Subgroups that have no uppercase letter denotation in
their column and that are also not referred to in any other column were not statistically different.

Highlights from the Results by Survey Sample

Respondents who were recruited to the survey through the Open Participation outreach effort were more likely to be active parks and
recreation users. More than 90% of respondents from both outreach efforts had used parks, playgrounds, picnic areas, natural areas
and/or trails, while 79% of Open Participation respondents had attended events and 35% had played in sports leagues compared to 65%
and 20% of Sampled respondents.

                                              Page 2
Fayetteville Parks System Master Plan Survey  Report of Results

Thinking about the purposes for providing parks and recreation facilities and programs, the top motivations for both groups of
respondents were to:

       · Provide places for people to spend time outdoors in nature
       · Contribute to a more beautiful community
       · Provide places for all to play
       · Protect the natural environment and promote environmental sustainability (for example, water quality, wildlife, air quality)
Those from the Sampled outreach were somewhat more likely to also name preservation of historic structures and sites, opportunities
cultural activities and personal enrichment/skills building classes and attracting visitors through special events and tournaments as
important purposes.

Open Participation respondents were more likely to be users of parks and recreation amenities and so it follows that they were more
likely to have experienced challenges in using the amenities. Specifically, they were somewhat more likely to have had major or moderate
problems with poorly maintained facilities, fully booked programs, poor connections for biking, long distances to parks and facilities, lack
of parking, too few features of activities of interest and poor accessibility for those with disabilities though the overall numbers reporting
issues were low.

Open Participation respondents were also more likely to say that there were too few amenities for picnicking, special events, water
recreation, open space, indoor gyms or courts, courts for racket sports, outdoor sports fields, indoor recreation centers and historic sites.

Asked to pick their top four priorities for the next 10 years for the Parks System Master Plan, two items were at the top for respondents of
both outreach efforts: community gardens and designated areas for natural environment preservation. Next for Sampled respondents
were City-maintained gardens, off-leash areas for dogs, and playgrounds, For Open Participation respondents water recreation and
swimming were prioritized. It should be noted that no one item was named in the top four by more than 29% of either respondent group.

Both groups had similar orders of preference for the types of swimming facilities they would like to see developed and they differed only
in that more of the Open Participation respondents expressed a strong preference. A majority of both put improving water quality at Lake
Fayetteville at the top of their list. Creating a natural swimming hole at White River and an outdoor water park with slides and lazy river
were second and third.

This was similar for rating the importance of actions Fayetteville could focus on for the next few years. Comparing the Address Sample to
the Open Participation, the ranking of importance was similar, but the intensity of importance was greater for the Open Participation
respondents. Topping both lists was:

       · Design or improve parks to support the environment (e.g., reduce flooding, improve air and water quality, etc.)
       · Preserve and connect more natural areas

                                              Page 3
Fayetteville Parks System Master Plan Survey                                                                    Report of Results

       · Improve or build parks in underserved areas of the city

Asked to rank six principles to guide Parks system planning, respondents to the Sampled survey most strongly prioritized completing
underdeveloped parks and improving connectivity and focusing on renovating and enhancing existing resources. Open Participation
respondents were a bit more likely to support expanding by acquiring land, but also prioritized improving what they have.
